newsitem.title: USA: U.S. House tax chief insists ethanol subsidy to end.
newsitem.headline: U.S. House tax chief insists ethanol subsidy to end.

text.p: The U.S. fuel-tax break for ethanol must end in 2000, the chairman of the House Ways and Means Committee insisted Monday, saying he would not allow an extension to become law.
The Senate Finance Committee voted last week to extend the ethanol subsidy, now worth 5.4 cents a gallon at the fuel pump, to 2007 but gradually lower it to 5.1 cents.

"I believe that the extension that is in the Senate bill that came out of committee, if it survives the floor, will be removed in the conference committee," chairman Bill Archer, a Texas Republican, told reporters.
A House-Senate conference committee is the usual route to write a final version of major legislation.

Archer said the tax bill written by his committee sent "a clear message to the ethanol community there will be no extension beyond the year 2000, so they should not build new facilities...in expectation Congress might extend the subsidy."

The bill written by the Ways and Means Committee would reduce the ethanol subsidy to 5.3 cents a gallon and eliminate it in 2000, as now scheduled in law. One private analyst said the approach appeared to give paramount importance to ending the tax break. Most of the $4 billion in savings claimed on ethanol would follow elimination of the tax break.

Ethanol proponents have hoped to out-flank Archer, a longtime foe, by preserving the tax break in the Senate. They also have been cheered by statements of support for ethanol by leaders like House Speaker Newt Gingrich, Georgia Republican.
About five percent of U.S. corn output goes to ethanol. The home-grown fuel is a popular cause among farmers and brings millions of dollars in additional income to them.

During a news conference, Archer lumped ethanol among the group of costly and unneeded alternative fuels given tax breaks during the embargo-fearing 1970s. It was foolish, he said, to waste a valuable feed crop on an industrial application like fuel.

There might be some change in terminology in the ethanol language as the tax bill is prepared for debate later this week in the House, Archer said, but it would be aimed at ensuring an end to the tax break.
